notes:
Task and constraints: Rearrange words into the order specified by each word's trailing position digit.
Idea: `sortSentence` splits the sentence into tokens, uses each token's trailing digit as its one-based destination position, removes that digit, and joins the ordered words.
Technique and why it applies: The trailing digit directly identifies each word's output index, so sorting by lexical content is unnecessary.
Invariant: Each word is placed into the slot encoded by its final digit, so output order follows the original position markers.
Edge cases: Words have one trailing position digit; the marker is not part of the output word; positions are unique and cover the sentence.
Complexity: O(L) time and O(L) space for all characters and the ordered word collection.
complexity_reason: The trailing digit directly identifies each word's output index, so sorting by lexical content is unnecessary.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the sum of the bitwise XOR of every subset of nums.
Idea: The implementation either enumerates subsets and XORs their elements or uses the fact that each bit set anywhere contributes to half the subsets; align the note with its code path.
Technique and why it applies: XOR is evaluated independently for each subset, and summing those results matches the requested total.
Invariant: Each subset contributes its XOR value once, and the accumulated total sums across every subset.
Edge cases: The empty subset contributes zero; duplicates are distinct positions in subsets; the problem's array size bounds brute-force enumeration if used.
Complexity: O(n·2^n) time for subset enumeration or O(n) for the bitwise shortcut; space depends on whether subsets are materialized.
complexity_reason: XOR is evaluated independently for each subset, and summing those results matches the requested total.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count substrings of length three whose characters are all distinct.
Idea: `countGoodSubstrings` slides over every three-character window and counts it when its three characters are pairwise different.
Technique and why it applies: A fixed-size window checks all possible substrings of length three in linear time.
Invariant: Each window is checked exactly once, and the count equals the number of valid length-three substrings in the processed prefix.
Edge cases: Strings shorter than three have no windows; repeated characters within a window make it invalid; overlapping windows are counted separately.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: A fixed-size window checks all possible substrings of length three in linear time.

notes:
Task and constraints: Map each letter a..j to digit 0..9 and check whether the first two word values sum to the third.
Idea: Convert each letter in each word to its digit offset from `'a'`, concatenate those digits into an integer, and compare the first two values' sum with the third.
Technique and why it applies: Mapping letters to decimal digits reproduces the word-number definition before comparing the sum.
Invariant: Each word's numeric value is the base-10 concatenation of letter indices, including possible leading zero digits.
Edge cases: Letters range from a through j; leading zero digits are permitted and do not change the numeric value.
Complexity: O(total characters) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond temporary numeric strings.
complexity_reason: Mapping letters to decimal digits reproduces the word-number definition before comparing the sum.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if rotating the square matrix by 0, 90, 180, or 270 degrees yields target.
Idea: Compare the current square matrix with `target`, then rotate each cell from `(r,c)` to `(c,n-1-r)` and repeat for the four orientations.
Technique and why it applies: Trying all four possible quarter-turn orientations exhausts every rotation allowed by the problem.
Invariant: After each rotation, the working matrix represents the next 90-degree clockwise orientation of the original.
Edge cases: The zero-rotation orientation is included; square dimensions stay constant; return true as soon as any orientation matches.
Complexity: O(n^3) time for four O(n²) comparisons/rotations and O(n²) space if rotations allocate new matrices.
complexity_reason: Trying all four possible quarter-turn orientations exhausts every rotation allowed by the problem.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if every integer from left through right is included in at least one interval.
Idea: Mark each interval value in a bounded boolean array or set, then verify every integer from `left` through `right` is marked.
Technique and why it applies: Marking covered values and checking each requested integer directly handles overlapping intervals and inclusive endpoints.
Invariant: The presence structure records whether each value is covered by at least one interval.
Edge cases: Intervals may overlap; endpoints are inclusive; a value need only be covered once.
Complexity: O(total interval lengths + right-left+1) time and O(U) space for the bounded value universe.
complexity_reason: Marking covered values and checking each requested integer directly handles overlapping intervals and inclusive endpoints.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the largest-valued odd-number prefix of num, or an empty string if none exists.
Idea: Scan `num` from right to left and return the prefix ending at the first odd digit; if no odd digit exists, return the empty string.
Technique and why it applies: The rightmost odd digit yields the longest prefix with an odd final digit.
Invariant: The rightmost odd digit gives the longest prefix whose last digit is odd, and that prefix is the largest-valued odd prefix.
Edge cases: Leading zeros are preserved as part of the string prefix; no odd digit means no nonempty odd-valued prefix.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the returned substring.
complexity_reason: The rightmost odd digit yields the longest prefix with an odd final digit.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return ans where ans[i] = nums[nums[i]].
Idea: For each index `i`, append `nums[nums[i]]` to the output array.
Technique and why it applies: Direct nested indexing implements the required `ans[i] = nums[nums[i]]` relation.
Invariant: The output position `i` is assigned the element indexed by the input value at `i`.
Edge cases: `nums` is a valid permutation of indices; output has the same length as input.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
complexity_reason: Direct nested indexing implements the required `ans[i] = nums[nums[i]]` relation.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the array followed by an identical copy of itself.
Idea: Create a result containing the original array followed by the same values again, using list concatenation or a length-2n output fill.
Technique and why it applies: Copying the input twice directly produces the required concatenated sequence.
Invariant: The first half equals the input and the second half repeats it in the same order.
Edge cases: An empty input yields an empty result; the returned array has exactly twice the input length.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
complexity_reason: Copying the input twice directly produces the required concatenated sequence.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if every distinct character in s occurs the same number of times.
Idea: Count each character with a frequency map or fixed alphabet array, then check that all recorded positive frequencies are equal.
Technique and why it applies: Comparing nonzero character frequencies tests equality of occurrence counts without confusing absent characters with present ones.
Invariant: The frequency table stores each distinct character's total occurrence count; equality is checked across those counts only.
Edge cases: A single distinct character qualifies; absent alphabet slots must not be compared as frequencies; empty strings are excluded by constraints.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for a fixed lowercase alphabet, or O(u) for u distinct characters.
complexity_reason: Comparing nonzero character frequencies tests equality of occurrence counts without confusing absent characters with present ones.
